obtained.how: the agency's own free PDF (Wisconsin DNR web site), fetched with getsrc

bibliography.checked_against: the title page (PDF p. 1) and the foreword
bibliography.note: the title page reads "Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, November, 2015"; no place is printed, so "Madison" in the reference is not from the document (harmless). The foreword calls the authoring group the "Panfish Standing Team"; the title page says "Panfish Management Team", as the reference does.

claims.claim: Saprolegnia infected 38 % of eggs in solitary nests against 19 % in colonies (Côté & Gross 1993, via Neuswanger et al. 2015)
claims.quote: nests of solitary males (38%) than of colonial nesters (19%)
claims.conditions: bluegill, Lake Opinicon context (solitary nesters ≥ 3 ft from neighbours); the review gives the share of eggs infected, "significantly more" in solitary nests, possibly because colonial males fanned more

claims.claim: at Lake Opinicon 94 % of water-column brood predation was by bluegill themselves (Gross & MacMillan 1981, via Neuswanger et al. 2015)
claims.quote: Predation on bluegill nests from the water column was primarily by conspecifics (94%)
claims.conditions: Lake Opinicon, Ontario; pumpkinseed also ate bluegill eggs and larvae

claims.claim: snails and fishes (mostly bullheads) took 11 % and 7 % from the substrate (Gross & MacMillan 1981, via Neuswanger et al. 2015)
claims.quote: snails (11%, mostly Viviparous georgianus) and fishes (7%, mostly Ictalurus spp.)
claims.conditions: Lake Opinicon; "substrate-level predation"; the review does not say of what total the percentages are
claims.note: the review says "Ictalurus spp.", not "bullheads": "mostly bullheads" is the paper's gloss (check Gross & MacMillan before keeping it)

claims.claim: edge nests lost at least three times more than interior ones (Gross & MacMillan 1981, via Neuswanger et al. 2015)
claims.quote: brood losses from peripheral nests were at least three times greater than from interior nests

claims.claim: crayfish at 1.4/m² destroyed every nest in small colonies within four weeks in Michigan ponds (Dorn & Mittelbach 2004, via Neuswanger et al. 2015)
claims.quote: 1.2 crayfish per square yard destroyed all bluegill nests in small colonies
claims.conditions: Michigan ponds stocked with Orconectes virilis and O. rusticus; small colonies = ≤ 15 males; over a four-week period; bluegill then nested only inside crayfish exclosures
claims.note: the review gives 1.2 per square yard (it converted metric to English units, foreword p. 1): 1.2 / 0.8361 m² = 1.44/m², so 1.4/m² holds

claims.claim: Lepomis larvae at Lake Mendota and Lake Opinicon were much denser in shallow open water near the colonies than far offshore, and at the deepest Opinicon site density was 8 % of the inshore mean (Post, Rudstam & Schael 1995; Garvey, Herra & Leggett 2002; both via Neuswanger et al. 2015)
claims.quote: larval density at the deepest offshore site was only 8% of average inshore limnetic density
claims.conditions: Lake Mendota (9,831 acres) and Lake Opinicon (1,927 acres); larval sunfish densities "throughout the summer" higher in shallow limnetic areas near nesting colonies than in deep areas far from shore

claims.claim: young largemouth ate 58–93 % of littoral bluegill fry at Ridge Lake, Illinois (Santucci & Wahl 2003, via Neuswanger et al. 2015)
claims.quote: high consumption (58-93% of littoral zone bluegill fry) by abundant young largemouth bass
claims.conditions: 14-acre Ridge Lake, east-central Illinois; young largemouth (≤ age 3) averaged 179/acre in 1987–1989; early-season fry suffered most

claims.claim: at Lake Opinicon in 1998 a cooling from 70 to 64 °F (21 to 18 °C) right after the early larval peak was followed by poor survival of early cohorts (Garvey, Herra & Leggett 2002, via Neuswanger et al. 2015)
claims.quote: water temperatures declined sharply from 70˚F to 64˚F immediately following the peak of larval abundance
claims.conditions: Lake Opinicon, 1998; the peak of larval abundance was in late May; the review says "disproportionately low survival of early-season sunfish fry to the fall juvenile stage"
claims.note: the review says the peak "of larval abundance in late May" (not an "early" peak) and "sunfish" fry; 70 °F = 21.1 °C and 64 °F = 17.8 °C, so the conversion holds

claims.claim: predators raised the overwinter loss of 28-mm age-0 bluegill in Michigan ponds from 10 % to 39 %, and to 55 % with walleye alone (Schneider & Breck 1997, via Neuswanger et al. 2015)
claims.quote: 10% in seven control ponds without predators, 39% in ponds with some type of predator
claims.conditions: unstructured 0.5-acre experimental ponds stocked each fall for four years with 1.1-inch (27.9 mm) bluegill at 4,348–8,502/acre and juvenile walleye (19–45/acre) or adult yellow perch; 55 % (range 25–89 %) where walleye were the sole predator

claims.claim: poisoning bluegill nests with copper sulfate from 18 May to 9 August in four Michigan lakes of 80–200 acres (32–81 ha) left the autumn age-0 catch only marginally below that of control lakes (Beyerle & Williams 1967, via Neuswanger et al. 2015)
claims.quote: mean age-0 CPE was only marginally lower in treatment lakes than in control lakes
claims.conditions: enough copper sulfate to theoretically kill all eggs and fry at nest sites, from the onset of spawning (May 18) to its end (August 9); fall catch per effort of age-0 bluegill, highly variable; it was slightly higher in treated lakes the year after than the year before treatment

claims.claim: in 38 Midwestern ponds bluegill stocks of 112–168 kg/ha produced the most age-0 fish, with fewer at lower and higher stocks (Novinger & Legler 1978, via Neuswanger et al. 2015)
claims.quote: standing stocks of 100-150 pounds/acre produced the maximum densities of offspring by fall
claims.conditions: 38 Midwestern bass–bluegill ponds of 0.5–6.0 acres; age-0 densities from fall rotenone samples were "considerably lower" at lower and higher stocks

claims.claim: ~0.005/day under the ice, so ~40–50 % die over a first winter, as with predators present (Neuswanger et al. 2015)
claims.quote: 55% (range 25-89%) in ponds where walleye were the sole predator
claims.conditions: Schneider & Breck (1997) as summarized: age-0 bluegill in 0.5-acre experimental ponds with stocked walleye or adult yellow perch; 39 % with any predator, 55 % with walleye alone, 10 % without predators
claims.note: ~40–50 % sits within 39–55 %; the review gives no winter length, so the daily rate is the project's (0.005/d over ~120–145 days of ice gives 45–52 %). Cite it as Schneider & Breck 1997 (via Neuswanger et al. 2015), experimental ponds, not lakes.

claims.claim: the field's first winters lose ~40–50 % in all (Neuswanger et al. 2015) and winter predation is low
claims.source_value: the only first-winter loss in the review is from experimental ponds: 10 % without predators, 39 % with any predator, 55 % (25–89 %) with walleye alone; the loss was predation by overwinter-feeding walleye and yellow perch
claims.quote: Overwinter mortality of age-0 bluegills averaged 10% in seven control ponds without predators
claims.conditions: 0.5-acre unstructured ponds, 1.1-inch age-0 bluegill, stocked predators, four winters (Schneider & Breck 1997)
claims.note: not "the field" and not low predation: in this source winter predation is what lifts the loss from 10 % to 39–55 % ("Walleyes tend to feed over winter")

notes: A WDNR literature review (55 pp., November 2015) that converts metric to English units (foreword): every metric value the paper takes from it (1.4/m², 28 mm, 32–81 ha, 112–168 kg/ha) is a back-conversion, and all check. Every paper claim attributed to it (all 'via') is confirmed. The one correction is a code comment (fish3.js:2247), which calls Schneider & Breck's predator-pond result "the field's first winters" with "winter predation low": the source says the opposite. Also in the review: Cargnelli & Gross (1996) — early-season fry (first trimester) were 17 % of fry production but 40 % of recruits in spring 1994 (p. 9, PDF p. 10), which bears on the paper's "rose 231 %" (§3.6.5); Bain & Helfrich (1983) — 83 % of fish near Lake Caroline colonies with bluegill larvae in their guts were 1.5–5.0-inch bluegill (p. 7); Kelso (1972) walleye maintenance ration 0.40 %/d at 39 °F and 1.17 %/d at 68 °F (p. 11).
